pamphlet_excerpts: Students Archaeology Study: Students of archaeology study a variety of subjects, including many sciences.
Scientific Analysis Sites: The scientific analysis of sites and artifactsrequires a knowledge of geology, paleontology, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and statistics.
Interdisciplinary Programs: Interdisciplinary programs that combine archaeology withvarious other fields of study are common.
Historical Archaeologists: Historical archaeologists usually major in anthropologyor history.
step_by_step_procedure: Previous Experience Isoften: To work as a field archaeologist, previous experience isoften required (usually obtained by spending a summer in anarchaeological field.
Archaeological Field Schools: Archaeological field schools provide the best way to learn howto properly excavate and document archaeological sites, andalso to find out.
Begin Now Prepare: You can begin now to prepare for your college courseworkby taking all of the science, history, and language classes youcan.
Strong Communication Skills: Strong communication skills are vital to an archaeologist, so you’ll need a good grounding in writing, speech, and foreignlanguages.

They Aerial Photographs: They may use aerial photographs andpictures taken from satellites to homein on the places they are trying to find.
They Talk People: They talk to people living in the area, Measuring an obsidian artifact from thewho often have the deepest knowledge.
step_by_step_procedure: Nightfire Island Site: Nightfire Island site in Oregon Sites are sometimes found during surveys that may berequired before new roads, dams, apartment houses, or other.
Archaeologists Walk: Archaeologists walk the entirearea, looking for anything made by humans that is more than 50 years old.
They Dig Test: They may dig test pits or trenches in the pathwayof the proposed construction.
Artifacts Appear Site: If artifacts appear, the site may be excavated beforeconstruction machinery disturbs the area.

Stratigraphy Order Layers: Stratigraphy (the order of layers in a site) provides anotherdating method.
Artifacts Buried Deeper: Artifacts buried in deeper levels of a site areusually older than items above them.
step_by_step_procedure: Archaeologists Knowthe Age: If archaeologists knowthe age of one level, they can determine that artifacts beneaththat level were probably left at an earlier date.
Ways Estimating Ages: These ways of estimating the ages of artifacts are calledrelative dating techniques because the date of one artifact orsite is related to the date.
Among Dating Techniques: Among the most used dating techniques arethe following.
Its Carbon Type: After a plant or animal dies, its carbon 14 (a type of carbon) slowly decays into carbon 12.

(a) For EACH site you research, point it out on a map and explain how it became known to archaeologists. Describe some of the information about the past that has been found at each site. pamphlet_excerpts: Idea Relationships Objects: This idea of relationships between objects is important.
Think Little Parts: Think of all the little parts that go together to make asmartphone.
Individual Parts Out: If you take the individual parts out of a smartphoneand study each one separately, will that tell you how the phonefunctions?.
Parts Insidethe Phone: You must look at all of the parts in place insidethe phone to see how they work together.
step_by_step_procedure: Smartphone Archaeological: Like a smartphone, an archaeological site is a complicated package that must be opened carefully and studiedas a whole if we are to make sense.
Researcher Looks Few: A researcher who looks at only a few stone tools and afew kernels of corn might find that, by themselves, the artifactsreveal little.
Few Kernels Corn: A few kernels of corn found in a spacethat did not have a hearth or any other artifacts would suggestthat the room was probably a storeroom.
Compared Anisolated: Compared with anisolated find, artifacts foundtogether at a sitecan provide moreinformation aboutthe people wholived there andeveryday activitiesof.

Excavation Destroys Site: Excavation destroys a site, so data must be recorded before anartifact and its surroundings are disturbed.
Records Thatarchaeologists: The records thatarchaeologists make include site maps, photographs of featureslike houses and pits, and drawings of artifacts.
Accurate Records Kept: When accurate records are kept, archaeologists will be ableto study a site even if they were not present during the excavation.
step_by_step_procedure: Ideally Archaeologists Study: Ideally, archaeologists study and write up their findingssoon after a site has been excavated.
Researchers Future However: Researchers of the future, however, might want to use new tools and new methods toreexamine the data from an excavation.
Excavation Tools: The excavation tools used by archaeologists include shovels, buckets, wheelbarrows, trowels, whisk brooms, brushes, and wire screens.
Surveyors Instruments Large: Surveyors’ instruments are used at large sitesthat have many excavation areas.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission, assist a qualified archaeologist for at least eight hours with a project being worked on. Projects may include surveying, site monitoring, site stabilization, surface excavation, laboratory analysis, use of digital archaeological technology, or public outreach. Describe your involvement in the project, what you learned about archaeology, and the steps of archaeological inquiry. Note: Visiting an archaeological site will require advance planning. An archaeological site during study can be a dangerous place. While there, you will need to closely follow the archaeologist's directions and comply with all the safety procedures. Be aware of the changing conditions at the site. (b) With your counselor's approval, take part in a simulated archaeological project designed by a qualified archaeologist. The project must include the use of a simulated archaeological site including artifacts and features for the site. Using the steps of archaeological inquiry, analyze the artifacts and features and document the spatial relationships of the artifacts and features at the simulated site. Explain how the environment and time can affect the interpretation of an artifact and the overall archaeological site. Tell how you would share the results of your analysis with other researchers and the public. Note: To find out how to make a simulated archaeological site, talk with a professional archaeologist, trained avocational archaeologist, museum school instructor, science teacher, advisor from a local archaeology society, or other qualified instructor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Besure Haveyour Parentor: Before yougo online, besure you haveyour parentor guardian’spermission.
Archaeology Become: As you can see, archaeology has become an importantscience for exploring our past and preserving our heritage.
Visitor Centers Built: Visitor centers have been built at many archaeological siteswhere you can view artifacts and learn about the people whomade and used them.
Museums Schools: Museums, schools, and publicbuildings may also have exhibits that share with everyonethe knowledge gained by studying the past.
step_by_step_procedure: Archaeology Clubs: Archaeology clubs andprofessional associations promote the appreciation of the pastand help protect cultural resources.
Libraries Rich Source: Libraries are a rich source of information aboutarchaeology and ancient cultures.
Librarians Findbooks Science: Librarians can help you findbooks about the science of archaeology and about the peoplesand periods of the past that interest you.
Internet Offers: The internet also offers many opportunities for exploring theworld of archaeology via computer.
